2026-08-31ResearchAnalysis available

Texas Manufacturing Outlook Survey — August 2026

Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas

Read analysis

Texas manufacturers reported faster output growth in August. The production index rose to 16.1 and new orders to 22.0. Broader business assessments improved, while employment growth became less widespread. The raw-materials price index was 44.1 and the finished-goods measure edged lower to 22.7, consistent with more widespread input-cost increases than sales-price increases. Expectations for production over the next six months became more positive. These diffusion indexes summarise the responses of 69 Texas manufacturers, which leaves national coverage and the size of changes open.

Questions for further research

  1. Where did the jump in new orders originate? Compare respondent comments with national orders, energy project demand and export markets.
  2. What is the lag between material costs and output prices? Track final and input price balances and sector-level margins in subsequent releases.
  3. Does stronger output lead to jobs or higher utilisation? Compare hiring, hours and capacity use with order growth and payroll records.

Source sections: Current report, collection dates and results table for production, new orders, employment, prices and outlook.

Official source ↗

2026-08-31ResearchAnalysis available

How do monetary policy surprises affect household sentiment?

Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland

Read analysis

The authors find a state-dependent response of consumer sentiment to unexpected monetary tightening. Their baseline linear regression produces little reliable average response. When previous-month inflation is low, an upward rate surprise is associated with higher sentiment in the interacted estimates. When inflation is high, the response turns negative. The authors discuss differences in what households infer about economic prospects and the costs of restraint. Their baseline inflation split uses 0.2% monthly headline CPI, while robustness tests change the cutoff and sample. Rate shocks are measured in a short FOMC window and related to monthly sentiment, so the estimates link a market surprise to an aggregate survey rather than individual spending decisions.

Questions for further research

  1. Does the sign switch depend on the inflation threshold? Replicate the estimates with continuous inflation and expectations measures and test stability across different samples.
  2. How much of the event surprise contains information about the economy? Identify rate and information shocks using rate-equity co-movements and compare their associations with sentiment.
  3. Does the sentiment response predict spending? Trace household consumption and credit use by income and interest-rate exposure after comparable shocks.

Source sections: Monthly sentiment regression, inflation regimes, Tables 2–5 and conclusion.

Official source ↗

2026-08-28SpeechAnalysis available

In Our Time — Kevin Warsh at Jackson Hole

Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

Read analysis

At Jackson Hole, Chair Kevin Warsh made a judgment about the balance of risks. He saw employment conditions as broadly consistent with full employment, financial conditions as difficult to call restrictive and inflation as still too high. He cited a jobless rate of 4.1%, relatively low initial claims, strong business investment and private domestic demand, narrow credit spreads and active issuance. Housing and agriculture showed strain. Rising AI investment could expand capacity and productivity, but the speech left its timing, labour-market effects, financing intensity and distribution of returns uncertain.

Warsh focused on the breadth and pace of inflation as well as the headline rate. Twelve-month PCE inflation was 3.7% in the data he cited. He said 54% of the PCE categories he examined had risen by more than 3% over the previous year, above the corresponding pre-pandemic share cited in the speech. Better summer prints had yet to convince him that underlying inflation was returning promptly to target. Medium-horizon expectations and inflation swap compensation appeared stable in his assessment.

The speech also set out a communications preference. Warsh favoured limited reliance on guidance about future rates outside crisis conditions and wanted financial-market prices to carry independent information. He saw short rates as the main policy tool and put weight on the broad effects of credit and money. The speech offered a criterion for action, confidence that underlying inflation is moving towards 2% fast enough, while leaving the next vote open.

Questions for further research

  1. Which components best distinguish persistent inflation from a small number of supply shocks? Reconstruct the speech’s PCE breadth calculation by weight and by item, then test whether different thresholds and windows move with other trend measures.
  2. How did the emphasis on less rate guidance change what traders reacted to? Compare meeting-dated policy pricing and rate volatility around the speech with the same instruments around other communication, controlling for the scheduled data tape.
  3. Is financial restraint concentrated in rate-sensitive sectors? Combine the cited bank lending standards with household mortgage activity, issuance and refinancing terms to distinguish firm credit conditions from housing and agriculture.

Source sections: Preparing for Future Policy Conjunctures, forward guidance discussion, Key Principles, The Economy Today and footnotes.

Official source ↗

2026-08-27ResearchAnalysis available

Can fiscal, AI, or monetary news explain the rise in r-star?

Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco

Read analysis

The working paper compares models of the US natural real rate with movements in financial-market estimates around news events. Major fiscal events offered only a modest upward contribution in the exercise. Selected AI model releases were associated with an overall decline in the estimates, and long-term rates and market-based r-star estimates generally fell around FOMC meetings in the sample. Together these event types explain little of the measured rise. The interpretation depends on the dates chosen, the separation of risk premia and the idea that news is processed around discrete events. The authors allow for more gradual fiscal or technological information and suggest considering global saving and investment.

Questions for further research

  1. Do other measures of r-star move in the same direction? Compare market-derived results with macro models and inflation-protected yields under alternative term-premium estimates.
  2. Can gradual updating explain the weak event-study attribution? Add earnings calls, budget forecasts and adoption dates to distributed windows with controls for overlapping releases.
  3. Which global developments could account for the common increase? Compare the timing across economies with changes in fiscal issuance, foreign demand and saving-investment balances.

Source sections: SF Fed Working Paper 2026-19, Tables 1–4, event-study design, monetary-policy extension and Section 6.

Coverage: Reviewed sections focus on the event design, results tables and conclusion.

Official source ↗

2026-08-25SpeechAnalysis available

Perspectives on the economy — Susan Collins

Federal Reserve Bank of Boston

Read analysis

Susan Collins saw stable employment and continued expansion in the United States, with persistent inflation receiving most of her attention. Her most likely scenario expected the effects of earlier tariffs and energy shocks to wane if new tariffs remained limited and the Strait of Hormuz reopened to some degree. Mild policy restraint, higher longer-term rates and continued productivity gains could help disinflation. She viewed the June and July releases as encouraging but too volatile to establish a trend. The AI buildout could lift core goods prices in the short run. Collins was comfortable with the July hold and wanted evidence of durable progress. Her outlook depends in part on avoiding fresh supply shocks and keeping expectations anchored.

Questions for further research

  1. Which inflation measures would show that supply shocks are fading? Compare energy and tariff-exposed categories with the broader core distribution and long-horizon expectations.
  2. Where is mild monetary restraint visible in the economy? Compare mortgage and consumer borrowing, bank lending to firms and the sensitivity of business spending to long yields.
  3. What would make the productivity channel stronger than AI-related input pressure? Use industry productivity, costs and goods prices to compare AI-exposed sectors with industries further from the buildout.

Source sections: Full prepared perspectives PDF, pp. 1–4, especially Inflation Concerns and Implications for Monetary Policy.

Official source ↗ · Prepared remarks PDF ↗

2026-08-25ResearchAnalysis available

Ninth District businesses continue to grapple with high costs

Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis

Read analysis

This August release summarises July responses from 905 Ninth District businesses. More than half reported lower profits than a year earlier and about 43% reported raising retail prices by at least 5%. Contacts attributed higher costs to several sources including tariffs and materials, with some reluctant to pass them through. Less than half were hiring and many of those were replacing leavers. Six-month sentiment was mixed. The survey used a convenience sample, heavily weighted towards Minnesota. It provides a timely account of pressures on responding firms. Its percentages do not represent national estimates.

Questions for further research

  1. How do cost pressures translate into margins by sector? Compare respondents’ input exposure, price changes and operating margins with administrative data.
  2. Are tariffs separable from regional demand or weather effects? Match business locations and industry inputs to tariff changes and regional travel and spending patterns.
  3. Could the employment signal reflect sampling composition? Reweight the responses and compare them with independent job openings and payroll data.

Source sections: July General Business Survey write-up, cost, profit and hiring figures and sampling note.

Official source ↗

2026-08-24ResearchAnalysis available

Chicago Fed Survey of Economic Conditions — August 2026

Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago

Read analysis

The Seventh District survey’s overall activity index fell from +11 to +5. The release PDF described growth as near trend. Manufacturing activity remained positive at +20, though it slowed, and the nonmanufacturing index reached −2. Current and expected hiring balances weakened, and the 12-month capital-spending expectation index stayed negative despite improving. Both labour and nonlabour cost-pressure indexes fell. The indexes summarise how many contacts rated conditions above or below their usual experience. Their levels measure the breadth of responses within this survey.

Questions for further research

  1. Is the divergence between manufacturing and services broad based? Cross-check subsequent district and national business surveys by sector and respondent mix.
  2. Do weaker hiring plans appear in realised employment? Compare regional payrolls, hours and vacancies with the survey’s hiring balance.
  3. What explains lower cost-pressure breadth? Compare local supplier costs and wages with the survey’s responses to assess whether disinflation is durable.

Source sections: August release PDF, activity and cost-pressure charts, index construction note and official release schedule.

2026-08-19MinutesAnalysis available

FOMC minutes — 28–29 July 2026 meeting

Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

Read analysis

Minutes released on 19 August show the Committee held the federal funds target range at 3.50–3.75% at its July meeting. Beth Hammack, Neel Kashkari and Lorie Logan preferred a 25-basis-point increase. Most participants expected new data to help them assess inflation persistence. The staff projected lower headline inflation as gasoline prices fell and saw inflation around 2% in 2028. Participants placed greater weight on upside inflation risks, including the prospect that repeated energy and tariff shocks could change expectations and pricing.

Demand and supply effects from AI investment were both relevant. Participants noted that strong investment in data centres and related inputs could lift demand and prices before any wider productivity gains expanded supply. Some saw those prices as concentrated in a few categories, while others already saw broader pressure. Resilient consumption and stable employment supported a waiting decision, although some noted low job-finding and strains on lower-income households. The Desk review attributed much of the earlier rise in nominal yields to higher expected policy rates and reported little change in inflation compensation. Those observations refer to the interval before the July meeting. The minutes give no market move at their August release.

Questions for further research

  1. What would make the July dissent the majority view? Compare the next core PCE measures, price breadth, inflation expectations and workforce indicators with the evidence the minutes identify. Separate a fresh commodity-price increase from wider pass-through.
  2. How much of a tighter path was already priced before the minutes? Use meeting-dated fed funds futures, two-year Treasury yields and inflation swaps around the 19 August release. Distinguish changes to expected policy rates from a shift in inflation compensation.
  3. When could AI investment tighten financial conditions through credit? Use segment-level capital spending, financing disclosures and banks’ or private lenders’ exposures to test how a reassessment of AI-linked earnings might affect funding and demand.

Source sections: Staff Economic Outlook; Participants’ Views; Committee Policy Actions and recorded vote.

Official source ↗ · Official release date ↗

2026-08-18ResearchAnalysis available

Introducing trimmed imports and exports

Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City

Read analysis

The authors introduce trimmed measures of US import and export growth. They aim to isolate components that improve forecasts of aggregate trade from volatile series with weak predictive content. The official summary reports better out-of-sample errors at medium horizons, particularly four to 12 months, with reductions up to 15% in some comparisons. The figures describe a forecast evaluation. The realised trade flow still includes the trimmed items, and large temporary changes in those items can matter for a quarter’s national accounts.

Questions for further research

  1. Which components are repeatedly trimmed? Inspect the algorithm and the weights across estimates and test whether the same industries drive improvements.
  2. Do the gains survive new tariff regimes? Re-estimate sequentially with data vintages and compare errors before and after changes in trade policy.
  3. Does the trimmed signal improve GDP forecasts? Test how its use affects net-export nowcasts alongside actual shipments and inventory data.

Source sections: Research Working Paper 26-08, official summary and reported forecast comparisons.

Coverage: The author conclusions and headline forecast evidence come from the Bank’s working-paper summary. Detailed tables and implementation were not reviewed.

Official source ↗

2026-08-13SpeechAnalysis available

The mysterious US economy — Tom Barkin

Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond

Read analysis

Tom Barkin explored why consumption, business investment and a low unemployment rate had persisted through an extended series of shocks. The speech links resilience to employment, wealth gains among asset holders and changes in spending behaviour. Weak sentiment and lower real income point to the risk that resilience is uneven. The unemployment rate can stay low when both demand for new hires and growth in the labour force slow. Barkin judged that much of the observed productivity improvement followed the post-pandemic labour squeeze through firms’ operational changes. He left room for additional AI gains. These mechanisms affect his reading of inflation persistence and labour-market slack. The speech does not identify a fixed next move.

Questions for further research

  1. How dependent is consumption on households with asset gains? Compare spending growth and liquid savings by income and wealth, controlling for changes in wages and credit.
  2. Does the low-hire, low-layoff pattern raise the risk of a rapid unemployment change? Use transition rates out of unemployment and changes in labour-force growth to examine that scenario.
  3. How can productivity sources be disentangled? Compare timing of operational changes and AI adoption with output per hour at the industry level.

Source sections: Prepared remarks on demand resilience, the low-hire and low-layoff labour market, and persistent inflation.

Official source ↗

2026-08-06SpeechAnalysis available

Monetary policy and productivity — Alberto Musalem

Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis

Read analysis

Musalem considers whether monetary policy can foster productivity by supporting investment and innovation. He sees potentially large cumulative gains if a policy change raises long-run productivity. He argues that this possibility provides weak grounds for deliberately accepting more inflation. The payoff from easier money is uncertain, financing conditions differ by borrower, and persistently high inflation can make planning and investment harder. He describes himself as optimistic about AI while treating future productivity gains as uncertain for current policy. The remarks set out a framework for the trade-off, rather than an assessment of a near-term market move.

Questions for further research

  1. Which productivity investments are actually sensitive to policy rates? Compare investment by firm financing structure, internal cash flow and exposure to long-term funding costs.
  2. Would faster productivity show up in inflation before it changes expected returns? Track unit costs and utilisation, then separate demand generated by the buildout from subsequent supply gains.
  3. What would demonstrate a persistent investment effect from easing? Test exogenous financial-condition changes against capital deepening and productivity over sufficiently long horizons.

Source sections: Full prepared remarks, the investment case for easing, inflation trade-off and closing judgment.

Official source ↗

2026-08-04StatementAnalysis available

Monetary policy perspective: keeping an open mind — Anna Paulson

Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia

Read analysis

Anna Paulson supported the preceding FOMC hold. The labour market looked broadly stable. Lower energy prices had helped June headline PCE, while her estimate of underlying inflation after adjusting for tariff and energy effects was around 2.4–2.8%. She set out two plausible readings of the same economy. Moderate pay growth and weak housing activity pointed to some restraint. Healthy private demand and business investment suggested current settings might prove too loose to bring inflation down promptly. Anchored expectations gave her room to assess which mechanism mattered most. She placed greater weight on inflation risk and remained open to an adjustment once underlying inflation became clearer.

Questions for further research

  1. How sensitive is the underlying inflation estimate to the tariff and energy adjustment? Reproduce the calculation across different affected items and lag structures using the component data.
  2. Is weak housing evidence of broad restraint? Compare housing turnover and financing costs with consumption growth across income groups and capex outside the AI buildout.
  3. Could an apparently steady unemployment rate hide weakening hiring? Cross-check job-finding, layoffs and survey perceptions with labour-force growth and labour demand.

Source sections: Current Conditions, Balance of Risks, Implications for Monetary Policy and footnotes.

Official source ↗

2026-08-03ResearchAnalysis available

Mortgage lock-in: a review of the literature

Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta

Read analysis

The working paper reviews what happens when owners with low fixed-rate mortgages would have to finance a new home at a materially higher rate. Keeping the old mortgage can discourage both a sale and a move, affecting housing turnover and the allocation of labour. The reviewed studies use different data, designs and definitions of a move. The authors distinguish the financing advantage of keeping a particular loan from the direct effect of that loan’s payments on household cash flow. Those mechanisms need different empirical tests and can imply different responses to market rates. The review also examines portability, wider mortgage assumption and a delivery option. Their wider housing and labour-market effects remain open.

Questions for further research

  1. How much lost mobility is caused by replacing the loan rather than the payment on the old loan? Compare households with comparable mortgage costs but different feasible refinancing or assumption terms.
  2. Where is the supply response strongest? Match listings, sales and rental prices to the distribution of local outstanding mortgage rates and transaction costs.
  3. Would portability reduce broader labour-market costs? Assess worker mobility, job transitions and lender or investor pricing under a change to mortgage contract terms.

Source sections: Working Paper 2026-11, mobility and home-sales evidence, Table 1, policy options and concluding discussion.

Coverage: This note focuses on the paper’s discussion of mobility, sales, empirical designs and policy options.

Official source ↗

2026-08-03StatementAnalysis available

John Williams on inflation and the policy path — New York Fed interview recap

Federal Reserve Bank of New York

Read analysis

John Williams judged that policy was positioned to support further disinflation in the circumstances he described. He expected tariff and Middle East effects on inflation to diminish over the second half of 2026 and into the following year. The recap also shows the policy condition behind that assessment. A failure to return towards 2% would warrant a response. Williams described financial-market developments as part of transmission to households and firms. The recap provides neither the size of any adjustment nor an estimate of the probability of a particular decision.

Questions for further research

  1. What would indicate that disinflation had gone off-track? Check energy and tariff-exposed categories alongside broad core PCE and household and professional expectations.
  2. Which financial-market moves would affect the real outlook? Track mortgage rates, corporate spreads and bank credit conditions alongside changes in the expected policy path.
  3. How firm was the outlook for an unchanged rate? Compare the full interview, adjacent public remarks and meeting-dated OIS to distinguish conditional guidance from any market assumption.

Source sections: New York Fed’s published summary of the Reuters interview, including its inflation, conditional policy and transmission passages.

Coverage: The Bank’s first-party recap is used here. It reproduces selected remarks from the interview.

2026-08-19ResearchAnalysis available

Quarterly Financial Report – Second Quarter 2026

Bank of Canada

Read analysis

The Bank reported second-quarter net income of C$298 million and first-half net income of C$479 million. It retained the earnings to reduce its accumulated deficit. Higher term and overnight repo activity supported year-over-year interest revenue despite lower interest generated by investments.

During the first half the Bank continued purchases through term and overnight repos and Government of Canada treasury bills. The report presented these operations in its account of assets and deposit balances.

Questions for further research

  1. How did the composition of the Bank's short-term assets change as settlement balances declined? The financial-position discussion connects the change in deposits with investments and repos. Compare the detailed statements and the Bank's settlement-balance series to assess the maturity mix and the potential implications for funding-market liquidity.
  2. How much of the net-income improvement came from higher repo volumes? The income discussion attributes higher interest revenue in part to repos. Reconcile repo volumes, rates and investment maturities in the quarterly notes to separate effects of earning assets from interest expense.
  3. How persistent could the accumulated deficit be under different funding costs? The Bank retained net income to reduce that deficit. Use the report's balance-sheet notes and maturity schedule to test net-income scenarios and the point at which remittances could resume.

Source sections: Management overview, financial position and financial results. Fiscal data to June 30; the publication is dated August 19.

Coverage: Review covers management commentary and financial highlights. The underlying statements are unaudited.

Official source ↗

2026-08-13StatementAnalysis available

Trial of Government of Canada securities settlement fail fees

Bank of Canada

Read analysis

The Collateral Infrastructure and Market Practices Advisory Group and the Canadian Depository for Securities announced a September 8 start for the first stage of a fee trial on settlement fails in Government of Canada bonds and treasury bills. The stage was scheduled to last at least 18 months.

The trial calculates indicative fees and supplies fail statistics and participant reports. A subsequent decision by the Canadian Fixed-Income Forum would be needed to activate payments.

Questions for further research

  1. Which issues or tenors account for the most persistent fails during the trial? The first stage makes statistics available on Government of Canada bond and bill fails. Use CDS fail counts and auction issue identifiers to test whether settlement risk clusters in collateral relevant to pricing or hedging.
  2. Do participants change settlement behaviour when they receive indicative invoices? The notice specifies that reports and indicative fees are available during the first stage. Compare failures and indicative invoice exposure around implementation while accounting for seasonal settlement patterns and issuance.
  3. How would a decision to activate payments affect repo spreads for scarce collateral? The forum retained authority for any subsequent decision on actual payments. Compare security-level repo quotes and fails before and after any future activation to assess the prospective cost of financing short positions.

Source sections: Bank-hosted market notice, trial mechanics and decision authority.

Coverage: Joint market infrastructure notice hosted by the Bank. The notice describes trial design.

2026-08-26ForecastAnalysis available

Quarterly Report – April to June 2026

Banco de México

Read analysis

Banco de México raised its 2026 GDP growth forecast from 1.1% to 1.5% and reduced the 2027 forecast from 2.1% to 2.0%. It still estimated a negative output gap throughout its forecast. The report characterized the growth risk balance as tilted down amid uncertainty around trade negotiations and geopolitical developments.

The report also reviewed headline and core inflation forecasts, and kept its projection of convergence to the 3% target in the fourth quarter of 2027. The revised path reflected higher core inflation over much of the horizon and higher non-core inflation in the first three quarters of 2027 relative to the prior report.

Questions for further research

  1. What explains the upward 2026 GDP revision and slight downward 2027 revision? Table 1 compares both estimates with the previous quarterly report. Compare the growth fan chart, revised quarterly history and sector assumptions to distinguish a mechanical carryover from better underlying momentum.
  2. Which real-time data could narrow uncertainty about a negative output gap? The Bank projects a negative gap and notes the uncertainty of an unobserved measure. Use contemporaneous labour-market and capacity indicators with alternative potential-output estimates to test how sensitive the rate outlook is to the gap.
  3. How do near-term headline revisions change the inflation profile without changing the eventual objective? The inflation table retains the August 6 forecast, which revised the shape of headline and core inflation relative to the prior quarterly report. Compare the forecast table by quarter and component to identify which pressures could change rate expectations.

Source sections: Executive summary PDF, pp. 5–8, GDP growth Table 1, output-gap chart and inflation forecasts.

Coverage: Review covers the Bank’s published executive summary.

Official source ↗

2026-08-20MinutesAnalysis available

Governing Board minutes – August 6 monetary policy decision

Banco de México

Read analysis

All five voting members supported keeping the overnight interbank rate at 6.50%. The account distinguishes policy views within that vote. One member discussed a neutral stance, noted uncertainty about potential GDP and argued that slack was secondary for choosing the stance during potential supply shocks. Another emphasized that transmission was still helping disinflation and that the exchange rate suggested room to absorb changes in conditions abroad.

A separate argument for a hold was that it addressed persistent inflation components and external risks while leaving flexibility to reassess easing inflation pressure. The individual views are presented without identifying speakers in the discussion section.

Questions for further research

  1. How sensitive are conclusions about slack to potential-output revisions? A member noted that a lower estimate of potential GDP would imply a smaller gap. Compare the activity data available to the Board and different real-time potential-output estimates before relying on slack as a rate catalyst.
  2. What would establish that monetary transmission is continuing rather than fading? A member linked disinflation to ongoing transmission. Compare contemporary credit conditions, core components and the timing of prior rate changes to test how demand is responding.
  3. How much protection could the exchange rate offer against an external tightening shock? A member cited the exchange rate as evidence of a buffer. Examine timestamped peso, overnight-indexed swap and US-rate data around prior external surprises, controlling for simultaneous Mexican releases.

Source sections: Minutes, monetary-policy discussion and Votación, official printed pp. 11–14. Decision August 6, minutes released August 20.

Coverage: Review covers the policy discussion and voting section, excluding the full statistical annex.

Official source ↗

2026-08-06DecisionAnalysis available

Monetary policy announcement – August 6, 2026

Banco de México

Read analysis

The Governing Board unanimously held the overnight interbank target at 6.50%. From the first half of June to the first half of July, annual headline inflation declined from 3.55% to 3.10% and core inflation fell from 4.12% to 3.95%. The Bank projected a more gradual disinflation path and convergence to 3% in the fourth quarter of 2027, with inflation risks still skewed upward.

The Bank reported a second-quarter rebound after a first-quarter contraction. It assessed the economy as still having slack and viewed growth risks as tilted down.

Questions for further research

  1. How much of June-to-July disinflation reflected temporary non-core price moves? Headline inflation fell more than core between the stated fortnightly observations. Compare fortnightly CPI contributions and monthly seasonal patterns to test how much disinflation can persist.
  2. Which core components account for slower expected convergence? The decision retained an upside-skewed risk balance and projected convergence in Q4 2027. Use forecasts and actual services and merchandise inflation to distinguish slower trend disinflation from volatile monthly releases.
  3. How did the changes in the peso and local yields discussed by the Bank predate the release? The announcement compares prevailing market conditions with the preceding policy decision. Compare independently time-stamped TIIE swaps and peso quotes around the publication before attributing any move to the decision.

Source sections: Official statement pp. 1–2, activity, forecast table, risk balance and decision.

2026-08-05MinutesAnalysis available

Board minutes – Policy rate held at 12.00%

Banco de la República

Read analysis

The minutes record four votes to maintain the 12.00% policy rate and three for a 50-basis-point increase. The majority supported a pause to assess earlier tightening. Some members pointed to stable June core inflation and the influence of prices affected by weather and international shocks.

The directors favouring an increase emphasized the risk of broader inflation from El Niño, the limited change in the ex-ante real policy stance relative to a year earlier, and the risks of delaying further tightening. The minutes cited July analyst expectations of 6.6% for December 2026 and 5.0% for December 2027.

Questions for further research

  1. Which indicators are most informative about the lagged impact of prior rate increases? The majority paused to assess transmission from previous increases. Compare monthly credit, lending rates and activity with earlier policy moves to see whether the majority's rationale holds as the data arrive.
  2. How does the neutral-rate estimate change the real-rate-gap comparison? Supporters of a larger increase cited a broadly similar ex-ante real policy stance to a year earlier. Use the Bank's real neutral-rate research and like-for-like inflation expectations to see how assumptions affect conclusions about existing restriction.
  3. Which indicators distinguish a weather-driven relative-price change from general inflation? The two sides discussed supply-driven inflation and the possibility that it spreads. Use price diffusion, weather monitoring and inflation expectations to distinguish a sectoral shock from a shift that could affect the nominal policy path.

Source sections: Official minutes, opening vote and majority and minority discussion. Published August 5 for the July decision.

Official source ↗

2026-08-04ForecastAnalysis available

Monetary Policy Report – July 2026

Banco de la República

Read analysis

The technical staff reported June headline inflation of 6.1%, up from 5.6% in March, and June inflation excluding food and regulated prices of 6.0%. It described pressure from labour and production costs, firm household and public spending, and agricultural disruptions. Peso appreciation partly tempered price pressure.

The staff projected headline inflation of 6.9% at year-end 2026 and 4.3% at year-end 2027, against the 3% target. It also described expansion in consumption and capital-equipment investment. Growth was 2.2% year over year in the first quarter. The staff projected 2.5% growth for 2026 and 1.9% for 2027, with a weaker impulse from some recent demand drivers.

Questions for further research

  1. Which services are most responsive to higher labour costs? The report cites labour costs in discussing persistent inflation. Use sector CPI and wage series across services to test which prices could keep inflation high after agricultural disruptions fade.
  2. How do household and public spending contribute to the inflation path separately? The staff describes both sources of firm demand. Reconcile national accounts demand components and official fiscal execution data before attributing the projected inflation path to private consumption or fiscal support.
  3. What exchange-rate pass-through assumptions underpin the return toward target? The report cites recent peso appreciation as a partial offset and forecasts lower year-end inflation in 2027. European Central Bank

Read analysis

The account released in August records the July hold. Most longer-term inflation expectations were still near the 2% target, and members saw limited evidence of second-round effects. Staff attributed the rise in headline inflation largely to the energy supply shock, with little contribution from demand or fiscal policy. The June increase had already signalled a willingness to act, and the July discussion emphasised the value of assessing more evidence.

Some members would have accepted another increase. They saw persistent energy prices and unexpectedly resilient demand as raising the chance that firms would pass costs on, and judged that delaying could require more tightening later. The August publication reveals differences in the July discussion. It is distinct from the July rate announcement for an event study.

Questions for further research

  1. Would the account have changed the odds on the next decision? Compare euro OIS in narrow windows around the July statement and August account.
  2. Which costs were firms able to pass through? Compare producer, refining and consumer price series with activity.
  3. Were expectations still anchored across cohorts? Compare professional, market and household measures over equal horizons.

Read analysis

The Bundesbank assessed that Germany remained on a recovery path despite higher energy costs. The second-quarter flash estimate showed real GDP growth of 0.2% quarter on quarter. Revised first-quarter growth was 0.4%. Because the revisions arrived in late July, the Bundesbank’s June forecast had not incorporated the stronger preceding activity.

Exports helped sustain industrial production and sales. Manufacturing capacity was still low, and higher borrowing costs and uncertainty limited equipment investment. Locking in the rate or staying flexible? Mortgage refinancing around an interest rate shock

Bank of England

Read analysis

The authors use predetermined UK mortgage expiry dates around the September 2022 mini-budget rates shock to study refinancing choices. More borrowers shifted towards two-year fixes even when these were priced above five-year fixes. A 200 basis point rise was associated with a reduction of roughly two to three percentage points in average loan-to-value ratios.

Adjustable-rate borrowing increased, though most borrowers still chose two-year fixes. The authors interpret this as a preference for protection against rate risk coupled with a prospect of refinancing sooner if rates fall. Evidence of more near-term equity extraction under two-year fixes supports their interpretation. The results describe a historical shock and inform how fixed-rate rollover and desired flexibility might affect transmission.

Questions for further research

  1. Are refinancing choices driven by expectations or access constraints? Compare contracts, underwriting cutoffs and borrowers’ balance sheets.
  2. How would the results change under a differently sloped mortgage curve? Compare term spreads and fixing behaviour across rate shocks.
  3. When does reduced equity extraction reach consumer demand? Match borrower refinancing dates with spending and liquidity measures.

Source sections: Staff Working Paper 1,203 abstract

How do firms cope with economic shocks in real time?

Bank of England

Read analysis

The authors combine administrative and survey microdata in a pre-registered design to estimate firms’ responses before slower structural data arrive. In their application to the 2021–23 UK energy shock, energy-intensive firms passed on costs, accumulated cash and increased homeworking. The authors found little evidence of aggregate job losses or exits. Smaller firms drove much of the estimated pass-through and larger firms drove investment responses.

The study compares its early estimates with later survey data and applies the framework to the 2026 shock. Its channel-level results help frame the question of whether higher energy costs are arriving as higher consumer prices, lower margins or reduced investment. The estimated relationship is conditioned by firm exposure and sample, and the paper represents its authors’ research.

Questions for further research

  1. Were the same firms affected in 2026? Compare exposure, hedging and pricing across energy shocks in the underlying data.
  2. How credible is the identification of cost pass-through? Review the pre-registration, instruments and robustness to pre-existing sector trends.
  3. Are cash buffers or reduced investment the more important response? Track liquidity and capex by firm size and prior energy exposure.

2026-08-21ResearchAnalysis available

Productivity and inflation dynamics

Bank of England

Read analysis

Ludovica Ambrosino, Jenny Chan and Silvana Tenreyro distinguish a temporary improvement in the level of productivity from a lasting rise in its growth rate. A temporary improvement lowers marginal costs and raises potential output in their account. It places downward pressure on the price level during adjustment before inflation returns to target.

A lasting improvement raises expected permanent income, potentially lifting investment, consumption and the natural real interest rate. Inflationary pressure can result under some monetary policy responses if demand rises before the productive capacity arrives. For an open economy, the transmission also depends on the sector affected. These are conditional mechanisms from a staff paper.

Questions for further research

  1. How should policymakers tell a temporary improvement in productivity from a persistent rise in its growth rate? The authors assign different marginal-cost, spending and real-rate channels to those shocks.
  2. How early would investment and consumption respond to an expected increase in productive capacity? The abstract identifies the timing of anticipated demand versus realised supply gains as a determinant of inflation pressure.
  3. Which affected sectors would matter most for an open economy’s inflation response? The authors say the sectoral incidence of the shock and the composition of demand matter.

Source sections: Staff Working Paper No. 1,201; authors’ abstract. Review limited to the abstract.

Read analysis

Łukasz Postek and Małgorzata Walerych use two complementary sign-restricted Bayesian VARs to separate demand shocks that affect employment relatively strongly from those that operate more through activity within existing jobs. In their estimates, the first type explains more unemployment variation. The second type is more important for output, inflation and productivity. Both matter for hours per employee.

Their estimated contribution of the two shocks changes over time. The findings are sensitive to how shocks are defined and identified, so they motivate checking hours and productivity alongside employment when diagnosing demand in Poland. The researchers' estimates are distinct from the Council’s macroeconomic forecast.

Questions for further research

  1. How sensitive are the estimated shock contributions to the sign restrictions? Replicate the baseline and alternative models and compare posterior distributions and impulse-response ranges.
  2. Did hours or employment lead the adjustment in more recent shocks? Use comparable quarterly labour, price and output series to update the sample and test revisions and structural breaks.
  3. Which labour indicators add most to a contemporaneous inflation nowcast? Test the out-of-sample performance of hours, employment and productivity indicators using the available data vintages.

Source sections: NBP Working Paper 389, abstract, identification, results and conclusion. 31 August is the public RePEc dissemination date. The publisher PDF specifies 2026 without a day.

Ryozo Himino in Saitama: Japan’s Economy and Monetary Policy

Bank of Japan

Read analysis

Himino described four forces shaping Japan’s outlook. Higher oil costs put pressure on output and pushed prices up. AI-related demand supported output and prices, while currency weakness raised import costs with mixed effects on activity. Financial conditions remained supportive. He said the economy looked resilient in the Tankan, firms’ profits and business investment plans, even though confidence among households was weaker than actual spending. He interpreted wages and scarce labour as supports for consumption.

The speech explains why the 1% nominal policy rate can coexist with accommodation. With rising wages and prices, some borrowers can bear higher nominal payments than in deflation, while depositors may face erosion of purchasing power. Himino pointed to negative short and medium real rates, bank lending appetite and accelerating loan balances. His approach to future adjustments weighs the balance of these channels against the policy outlook. The outcomes he describes precede the speech.

Questions for further research

  1. How much of the move in import costs was due to exchange rates versus commodity prices? Compare import prices in yen and foreign-currency terms and track energy subsidies and firms’ input costs.
  2. Is the nominal rate level a good gauge of household cash-flow pressure? Compare wage growth, deposit interest and variable-rate mortgage payments across age and leverage groups.
  3. Is the AI-led investment impulse visible outside large exporters? Check orders, Tankan investment plans and profits by firm size and industry.

Source sections: Sections I–II, four macro drivers, the discussion of real borrowing rates and charts 6–7.

The PBOC’s second-quarter report describes maintaining a moderately loose stance under a more uncertain external backdrop. It cites 4.7% year-on-year GDP growth in the first half. It pairs ample system liquidity and reduced financing costs with targeted tools for innovation, smaller firms and other preferred sectors. It describes adding overnight reverse repos and narrowing the temporary repo and reverse-repo band from 70 to 50 basis points. The outlook keeps operations and fiscal coordination flexible and supports orderly moves in the managed RMB float. The summary supplies no market pricing around publication.

The authors use pension subscriber and labour-force survey data to study young workers during the spread of AI. Reserve Bank of Australia

Read analysis

McKay decomposes the household consumption deflator into labour costs, business owner returns, dwelling rents, import prices and net taxes. The method maps costs at industry level through input-output and consumption weights. Graph 1 compares contributions during the recent inflation episode with an illustrative benchmark of costs growing at 2.5%. The article finds that import prices and business owner returns accounted for more of the rise early in the period, while labour costs and dwelling rents became more important from 2023.

The article explains why the deflator and headline CPI moved differently. They measure owner-occupier housing differently, and some subsidies affect the prices households pay in the CPI while leaving listed prices used for the deflator unchanged. The decomposition is an accounting approach to the sources of measured price growth. Its results can guide tests of inflation persistence, with separate evidence needed to identify whether a given cost contribution reflects excess demand, a supply shock or both.

Read analysis

Jacobs describes the RBA’s transition toward reserves driven by banks’ demand rather than past asset purchases. As pandemic-era bonds run off, the RBA’s weekly full-allotment repo operations can expand if money-market rates create an incentive for lenders to obtain reserves. The amount of reserves can then react to demand while the asset side shifts from long-term bonds toward short-term repo. Jacobs says a smooth transition depends on the ability to supply liquidity flexibly rather than a fixed reserve target.

If official repo activity grew enough to affect functioning in private markets, the RBA could use additional liquidity instruments, such as FX swaps or purchases of short-term government securities. The RBNZ analytical note constructs separate measures of foreign and domestic macroeconomic uncertainty and estimates their associations with the New Zealand economy. The two series move together to a substantial degree. The authors interpret that co-movement as consistent with foreign developments contributing to domestic uncertainty. For both categories, estimated responses imply weaker GDP and a higher CPI after an uncertainty increase.

This pattern raises a policy trade-off because the inflation and activity implications point in different directions. The estimated effects belong to the authors’ identification method and sample. The bulletin argues that low job loss was doing more to hold down unemployment than robust hiring. The authors estimate a job-finding rate of 34%, below 39% in 2019, and show longer spells out of work. Employer hiring and separation data point to a similar slowdown in flows. 2026-09-23ResearchAnalysis available

Testing for contemporaneous exogeneity in linear time-series models

Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta

Read analysis

Dovonon and Gospodinov develop a specification test for whether a time-series regressor is contemporaneously exogenous. They construct an expanding collection of moments from the regressors themselves. The method can test a single subset of regressors under its assumptions without requiring external instruments. They apply it to measures of labour tightness and slack in alternative Phillips-curve specifications. This matters for macro research because slack can move in response to the same forces that move inflation. A regression coefficient alone cannot identify policy transmission under such simultaneity. The paper supplies a model diagnostic. Its assumptions about sample size, moments and regressor dynamics matter for interpreting the test.

Questions for further research

  1. Are the candidate slack proxies equally exposed to feedback? Use the paper’s empirical specifications to compare results for labour tightness and the unemployment gap over the same vintage.
  2. Is the test informative in short post-pandemic samples? Use the documented simulations as a starting point and vary sample size, persistence and shocks.
  3. Does choosing a better-specified measure change the inflation forecast? Compare rolling out-of-sample errors and policy-scenario responses for models using the tested proxies.

Source sections: Working Paper 2026-14, abstract, Phillips-curve applications and Section 8.

Coverage: The note focuses on the test, the application and the conclusion. It does not assess every proof or simulation.

Governor Christopher Waller was open to holding the funds rate if August inflation confirmed the preceding disinflation. An anticipated measurement change might reduce reported inflation, independently of underlying price-setting. Energy, tariffs and AI equipment costs remained upside risks.

The September decision was therefore conditional on incoming prices. Waller distinguished explaining an existing vote, describing his data-dependent response and using guidance as a policy tool at the effective lower bound. The remarks describe his personal vote criteria and provide no committee commitment.

  1. What portion of the GDP downgrade stems from household spending versus other cyclical components? The Bank cites Q2 composition and weak early Q3 indicators. Compare the Bank's sector forecasts with national accounts and early Q3 consumption to estimate the weight of rate-sensitive domestic demand.
  2. Which services components remain elevated despite slowing overall prices? The report contrasts easing headline inflation with services persistence. Compare CPI subindexes with wages and service activity to test which components could slow the return toward the target.
  3. What offset higher expected inflation and a larger output gap at the forecast horizon? The report identifies recent inflation surprises and a near-term reversal in oil prices as downward offsets. Use the report's forecast decomposition and alternative scenarios to estimate which offsets would still hold if oil prices and expectations moved together.

2026-09-21SpeechAnalysis available

The challenge of innovation — Fabio Panetta

Banca d'Italia

Read analysis

Panetta argued that AI can improve analysis and change the economy the central bank is trying to forecast. Near-term investment can boost demand for scarce compute, energy and skills before supply is ready. The longer-term supply effect depends on adoption and the productivity gains that follow. The timing of demand and supply shifts therefore determines the inflation consequences.

How gains are distributed also matters. New tasks that strengthen labour incomes can reinforce consumption and investment. Automation that increases insecurity may raise precautionary saving and offset some investment demand. Panetta discussed national differences in diffusion and the potential for larger firms to capture gains sooner. The speech presents mechanisms and cites research estimates. It makes no commitment about the next rate setting.

Questions for further research

  1. Which input constraints could bind before productivity gains arrive? Compare energy, compute and specialist wages with adoption estimates.
  2. Are household responses affecting consumption yet? Track savings and jobs by exposure to automation and new tasks.
  3. Which national or sector differences matter for policy? Compare firm adoption, output and wage distribution across countries.

Source sections: Section 3 and its subsections on aggregate demand and international divergence

2026-09-04SpeechAnalysis available

The institutional form of independent central banks: from history to contemporary challenges — Andrew Bailey

Bank of England

Read analysis

Andrew Bailey sets central bank independence in the history of efforts to constrain arbitrary power and treat stable money as a public good. For the Bank of England, he locates authority in Parliament’s role in setting objectives and powers and retaining authority to alter the framework. The central bank’s ability to act with insulation from short-term political pressure depends on that delegation.

Bailey links institutional durability to open explanations, public engagement and accountability to the House of Commons Treasury Select Committee. He recognises different effects on borrowers and savers as well as the role of trust in the financial system. The speech addresses how monetary authority is exercised and scrutinised.

Questions for further research

  1. How should Parliament distinguish scrutiny of decisions from changes to the Bank’s mandate? Bailey identifies a formal parliamentary role in setting and revising the framework and an ongoing accountability role for the Treasury Select Committee.
  2. How can the Bank communicate distributional effects while explaining how a decision serves its statutory objectives? The speech acknowledges that borrowers and savers experience rate decisions differently and argues for clear public explanations.
  3. What practices help central banks maintain broad public trust when different groups challenge the same decision? Bailey discusses opposing criticisms and identifies transparent decisions and public engagement as safeguards for institutional legitimacy.

2026-09-10SpeechAnalysis available

Kazuyuki Masu in Fukui: Economic Activity, Prices, and Monetary Policy in Japan

Bank of Japan

Read analysis

Masu argued that negative short real rates deserved early attention in an economy that had left deflation. At the time the 1% policy setting was below the lower end of his illustrative 1.1–2.5% nominal neutral range. He built that range by adding the 2% objective to a broad set of model estimates of the natural real rate. He cautioned that neutral could not be pinned to a single number. Persistently negative short real rates could support leverage, encourage businesses to bring investment forward and reduce the purchasing power of households’ savings.

Different shocks implied different policy trade-offs. The Middle East shock affected output as well as input prices; a weaker yen amplified imported prices but was not itself the policy target. AI demand offered an offset for activity and raised some prices. Food inflation could persist beyond rice or energy because of distribution and packaging costs. The evidence and rate assessment represent Masu’s views as expressed in September.

Questions for further research

  1. How sensitive is the rate gap to estimated expectations and methods? Compare several measures of expected inflation and trend growth when constructing a range of real and neutral rates.
  2. Is rising food inflation spreading after removing narrowly volatile items? Track processed-food prices, distribution and packaging costs and selling-price revisions.
  3. How exposed is Japan if global investment in AI equipment decelerates? Compare semiconductor materials and equipment exports, orders and corresponding profit sensitivity.

Source sections: Price risk sections, the interpretation of charts 7–8 on real and neutral rates, and policy conduct.

The CBC kept its discount rate at 2.00%, secured refinancing at 2.375%, and temporary accommodations at 4.25%. It saw contained inflation despite a substantial upward adjustment to its growth outlook. Technology exports and investment supported an 11.48% growth forecast for 2026, with the Bank projecting 5.82% for 2027 against a high base. Core and headline forecasts remained just above 2% for 2026 and were expected to ease below 2% in 2027. Its assessment of the external energy shock and inflation outlook supported a hold while monitoring global conditions, capital flows and domestic prices.

The board separately eased a targeted constraint: the second-home mortgage loan-to-value ceiling rose from 60% to 70%, and a construction-timing affidavit for land loans was removed. The changes took effect 18 September. The CBC linked the adjustment to a decline in banks’ real estate lending concentration and improvements in internal controls. The mortgage decision could affect particular borrowers independently of the policy rate. The statement also retained scope for FX intervention during disorderly conditions.

Questions for further research

  1. How much does the growth forecast depend on a few AI-related industries? Compare exports, output, investment and household demand by industry using the same release vintage.
  2. Does loosening second-home LTV ceilings alter financing availability? Check new mortgage LTV, approval rates, pricing and credit concentration around implementation.
  3. What would unsettle the below-2% inflation forecasts for 2027? Compare the assumed oil path, energy relief and service-price persistence with incoming component data.

Source sections: Sections II–V: forecast, policy-rate hold, selective credit controls, and FX framework.

Read analysis

The MAS review, using information available through 17 September unless stated otherwise, sees higher global sovereign yields, fiscal pressure and persistent input costs as sources of financial risk. AI investment and exports can support earnings and activity in the economies most exposed to the technology cycle. The same exposure makes those economies vulnerable if projects or valuations disappoint. The review distinguishes the effects of higher refinancing costs on sovereigns and private borrowers from the potential risk of a more abrupt change in asset prices.

MAS finds generally sound Singapore corporate, household and bank balance sheets. Borrowing costs had eased domestically and credit spreads had narrowed. Stress tests suggest most borrowers and financial institutions have buffers, while highly leveraged firms and a subset of lower-liquidity borrowers remain vulnerable. The resident credit-to-GDP ratio was 133% in Q2, down slightly from 134% in Q4 2025 and below trend. MAS says the countercyclical capital buffer will stay at 0% in 2027. This is a banking resilience assessment and a macroprudential setting. Its stress-test findings are conditional on scenario design.

Questions for further research

Bullock explains why the Board raised the cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.60%. She describes pressure from renewed increases in global energy prices and inflation in technology-related goods, alongside concern about domestic capacity and weak productivity. In the Q&A she explains that weaker supply growth affects how far demand can expand without generating price pressure. The deterioration in the inflation outlook shifts how the Board weighs the trade-off with employment, while it continues to pursue both objectives.

The Governor says rates could rise again if needed. The remarks clarify the motives behind the decision and the conditional nature of further action. To estimate any market information attributable to the press conference, use the conference’s separate scheduled window after the policy statement rather than attributing the entire day’s price move to her Q&A.

Questions for further research

  1. What did the press conference add about future rate moves? Compare market pricing immediately after the written decision with pricing during and after the press conference.
  2. How much of the inflation revision could reflect slower potential growth? Compare productivity data, underlying prices and activity against previous staff assumptions.
  3. Does weaker demand make the stated trade-off easier in later quarters? Track spending and hiring responses at different policy lags and look for persistent wage and price pressure.

Source sections: Opening statement and Q&A on productivity, capacity and policy transmission

2026-09-22SpeechAnalysis available

Michele Bullock: Fireside chat at CEDA

Reserve Bank of Australia

Read analysis

Bullock describes the policy trade-off when adverse supply shocks raise inflation and simultaneously weaken activity. Repeated shocks matter because a sequence of price increases can change the inflation expectations of households and firms. She says monetary policy can limit the propagation of those shocks through demand, price setting and expectations. That is different from offsetting the first-round change in a relative price.

She also discusses the pressure of mortgage costs on household budgets and the difficulty of explaining the distinction between those costs and consumer-price inflation. For productivity, she sees possible benefits from AI over time alongside risks during a transition, including changes in labour-market matching. Her comments concern the policy objective and medium-term trade-off. The market question is whether her emphasis on expectations and supply implied a materially different response from what investors had priced.

Questions for further research

  1. Are repeated shocks changing price-setting behaviour? Compare price plans and wage settlements over successive episodes, controlling for import-cost exposure.
  2. Would lower household confidence magnify transmission? Compare spending in indebted and less indebted households and track home loan repricing.
  3. Does the speech materially change the policy message since the testimony? Compare wording on second-round effects with the 18 September testimony and check price changes around the event.

Source sections: Governor’s transcript, supply-shock, inflation-expectations and productivity passages

The Future of Banking Study: scenarios for New Zealand in 2035

Reserve Bank of New Zealand

Read analysis

The RBNZ study explores how banking in New Zealand could look under three scenarios through 2035. Its scenarios span continued incumbent dominance, a larger role for digital challengers and greater use of platforms that distribute or combine banking services. The horizon and scenarios are inputs for supervisory planning. They do not give probabilities or a central forecast for industry shares.

Competitive entry and new technology could improve efficiency and access, while fragmentation of banking services could create dependencies on concentrated providers and activities outside existing supervisory coverage. The study draws on research, scenario development and engagement. An investor could use the scenarios to identify which parts of the banking value chain are exposed to changes in customer access, funding and distribution, then look for adoption evidence separately.

Questions for further research

  3. What operational risks would become more concentrated under a platform model? Review provider dependencies and how continuity requirements and service arrangements are structured.

Karen Silk: Securing the future, the role of the repo market

Reserve Bank of New Zealand

Read analysis

Silk explains how government bond-backed repo helps distribute cash and collateral, supports trading in securities and transmits the policy rate through wholesale markets. The speech introduces the role of regular liquidity provision and reports that term operations can lend at OCR plus 10 basis points for seven and 28 days.

2026-09-02DecisionAnalysis available

OCR increased by 25 basis points to 2.75%

Reserve Bank of New Zealand

Read analysis

The Monetary Policy Committee reached consensus on raising the OCR by 25 basis points to 2.75%. Its record says that further increases were possible under the central outlook. Headline inflation remained high, but most core measures were inside the 1–3% target band and inflation excluding vehicle fuel was 2.9% year on year in the June quarter. The committee expected falling fuel-related contributions, spare capacity and reduced stimulus to bring inflation back to the 2% midpoint in late 2027.

Recovery was uneven. Strong export prices and resilient trading partners were supporting activity and investment in some regions. Domestic spending and labour markets were weaker, and the positive spillovers from exports to households had been limited. The committee judged gradual withdrawal of stimulus a way to protect the target while avoiding an abrupt later adjustment. It noted that wholesale and loan rates had risen partly on market expectations of future moves. The size of the surprise on 2 September remains an empirical question.

Questions for further research

  1. How much of the hike and conditional path was in NZD rates? Compare meeting-dated quotes around the official 2 pm NZT release and distinguish the decision from the forecast.
  2. Could export strength feed into domestic demand faster than projected? Compare regional job, capital spending and household income measures with export and tourism earnings.
  3. Is lower fuel inflation sufficient for durable disinflation? Track non-tradables, inflation expectations and survey measures of cost pass-through.

Source sections: Media release and summary record, especially financial conditions, risk and decision

2026-09-02ForecastAnalysis available

Monetary Policy Statement, September 2026

Reserve Bank of New Zealand

Read analysis

The RBNZ projects annual inflation returning to within the target band in the June 2027 quarter and close to the 2% midpoint by late 2027. Lower fuel prices and the base effect of the earlier increase are important to that path, which is conditioned on oil futures. The negative output gap and reduced stimulus are expected to restrain underlying price pressures. The statement projects annual September-quarter CPI at 3.9%. This figure is a contemporaneous forecast rather than a subsequent observation.

Box B illustrates the costs of bringing inflation back into the band more quickly. In its model scenario the OCR peaks around 4.5%, returning inflation to the band earlier, after which inflation falls below 2% as fuel effects fade. The model also shows weaker activity and a higher unemployment rate. The Box compares scenarios under its assumptions, not a proposed central OCR path. The forecast’s market relevance depends on whether oil, spare capacity and pass-through evolve as envisaged.

Questions for further research

  1. How sensitive is the return-to-target date to the futures curve? Compare subsequent energy curves and the exchange rate with the conditioning assumptions used on 2 September.
  2. Can the gradual strategy contain price persistence as fuel base effects fade? Monitor expectations, non-tradables inflation and wage growth alongside the headline measure.
  3. How robust is the faster-hike scenario’s employment cost? Compare the Box B results across alternative pass-through and monetary transmission assumptions.

Source sections: Key projections, the faster-hike counterfactual in Box B and Figure 5.1. Selected chapters reviewed.

Waller attributed his support for September’s quarter-point increase to a shift in risks over several months. Labour conditions had stabilised and inflation remained above target. 2026-10-01SpeechAnalysis available

Michelle Bowman · Modernizing Financial Regulation: Initial Observations from eSLR

Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

Read analysis

Bowman argued that the supplementary leverage requirement had become a binding constraint for some large bank dealers and that recalibration could support balance-sheet-intensive Treasury intermediation. She cited supervisory data showing dealer Treasury holdings rose from about $600 billion to over $700 billion by the end of April, with more growth among banks that had smaller buffers under the prior rule.

She also cited market outreach and indicators such as narrower spreads and lower volatility around auctions. These are preliminary observations, and the reported change in holdings has a different evidentiary status from statements by individual market contacts. The suggested mechanism is more capacity for dealers to absorb Treasury supply, with implications for liquidity and cash–futures positioning.

Questions for further research

  1. Can holdings growth be attributed to the calibration? Compare affected and less constrained dealers, conditioning on issuance and market volatility.
  2. Does capacity remain available in stress? Compare quote depth, repo terms and dealer holdings on the busiest auction or volatility days.
  3. How has exposure moved between dealers and leveraged funds? Cross-check Treasury positions, repo funding and futures exposures over the same period.

Source sections: Binding leverage requirements, supervisory data, market outreach and footnotes

2026-10-28ForecastAnalysis available

Monetary Policy Report—October 2026

Bank of Canada

Read analysis

The October outlook projects inflation above 3% through much of 2027 and near 2% by mid-2028. The Bank judged that sustained oil and refinery pressures were affecting Canadian firms’ costs, with broader consumer-price effects expected as those costs passed through. The same energy shock supports investment and exports through Canada’s commodity sector while reducing purchasing power for households and raising costs for energy users.

The Bank forecasts 1% annual growth in 2026 and 2% in both 2027 and 2028. Stronger midyear activity improved the growth outlook versus July. Tariffs and uncertainty still constrain exports and investment in affected sectors, while housing remains weak. The report’s outlook is conditional on its trade, energy and pass-through assumptions.

Questions for further research

  1. What would bring CPI back to target faster? Re-run the report’s assumption with a faster fall in oil and refinery margins, then check whether pricing behaviour changes.
  2. How exposed is the growth upgrade to tariffs? Track trade by industry, capital spending plans and US demand in the sectors identified by the report.
  3. Is housing the main source of downside growth risk? Compare mortgage renewals, resale activity and residential investment with the report’s projected path.

Source sections: Overview and report chapters on outlook and risks

Bank of Canada

Read analysis

The Bank raised the overnight-rate target to 2.50%, with the Bank Rate at 2.75% and the deposit rate at 2.45%. Persistently high energy prices and refinery margins had kept headline inflation near 3% since April. The Bank saw signs of broader cost pressures, including transport and imported industrial and electronics inputs. Core measures remained near 2%, but its surveys indicated more firms expected to pass through higher input costs.

The Canadian economy also entered the second half of 2026 stronger than the Bank had forecast in July. The Bank nevertheless projected a tariff-related slowdown in the fourth quarter and described some excess supply. The decision addresses the risk of persistent inflation as activity recovers, with the next steps contingent on incoming data. The release describes recent rates and currency conditions without providing an event-window market response.

Questions for further research

  1. How fast are input costs reaching consumer prices? Use the Bank’s business surveys and CPI component contributions to distinguish direct gasoline effects from broader pass-through.
  2. How much has domestic slack narrowed? Compare job vacancies, hours worked and output-gap estimates with the October forecast.
  3. How much tightening was priced before the release? Match the original release time to CORRA pricing and CAD observations around the announcement.

Four directors voted to retain the 12.25% policy rate and three preferred a 25 basis point increase. Analyst expectations for the end of 2026 edged higher to 6.9%, and two-year expectations remained near 4.0%. Measures inferred from government debt remained away from the 3% target.

The October release records a divided September rate increase. Four directors chose a 25 basis point increase to 12.25%, two preferred a hold and one wanted a 50 basis point increase. Read analysis

The Governing Council left the deposit facility rate at 2.50%, the main refinancing rate at 2.65% and the marginal lending rate at 2.90%. 2026-10-09SpeechAnalysis available

When the policy mix meets supply shocks — Agnès Bénassy-Quéré

Banque de France

Read analysis

Bénassy-Quéré argued that supply shocks complicate coordination because inflation rises as output weakens. Temporary energy support can cushion incomes and reduce the measured CPI peak, while broad fiscal support can sustain demand and increase financing pressure. Higher nominal growth does not guarantee improved fiscal space when spending is indexed and debt service rises. Support that eases a bottleneck can affect inflation differently from general demand support.

France’s energy shield is the main case study. The Banque de France research cited in the speech estimates that the shield reduced inflation by around 2.6 percentage points in 2022. Part of that effect reversed in subsequent years. The evidence leaves open whether a lower peak also moderated wage and expectation persistence. Comparisons between French and aggregate euro area prices are descriptive and cannot identify the shield’s full long-run impact on their own.

Questions for further research

  1. How much of the lower measured inflation reflected postponed price increases? Review the shield study’s counterfactual, regulated tariff schedules and pass-through after support was wound back.
  2. Did a lower inflation peak change bargained wages and expectations? Compare sector wage deals, household expectations and cross-country evidence controlling for other shocks.
  3. What is the cost of financing renewed support? Assess the programme’s primary balance effect, debt maturity and sensitivity to long yields.

Source sections: Slides 5–8 and the France case study.

Diagnostic Challenges for ECB Monetary Policy — Philip R. Lane

European Central Bank

Read analysis

Lane set out three tests for a policy response to the energy shock: the inflation outlook and its risks, underlying inflation, and the strength of transmission. September headline inflation was 3.8% and the energy component was up 18.8% year on year, while non-energy inflation was 2.3%. The underlying mix had nevertheless changed since late 2025, with non-energy goods inflation higher and food and services inflation lower. Lane saw little evidence at that point of the unusually fast repricing mechanisms observed in 2022.

The September staff projections anticipated lagged pass-through lifting non-energy inflation to 2.6% in 2027 before it returned to 2.3% in 2028. He argued that financial conditions matter twice: tighter conditions directly depress demand, and they change how strongly a given monetary stance affects the economy. The decision therefore depends on whether energy costs broaden and on whether other financial conditions strengthen or offset policy restraint.

Questions for further research

  1. Is repricing becoming faster or broader in response to energy? Check item-level HICP price adjustment frequencies, services inflation and the underlying inflation measures cited in the speech.
  2. Is lagged energy pass-through consistent with the staff path? Compare the September projection assumptions with wholesale energy, producer prices and reported pricing intentions.
  3. How much of tighter financial conditions is delivering restraint independently of the policy rate? Track the ECB’s cited conditions indices and decompose changes in credit costs and market rates.
